title: Quantum capacity of the qubit depolarizing channel
formal: Determine the unassisted quantum-capacity function \(Q(q)=Q(\mathcal D_q)\) for every real \(q\in[0,1]\), where the qubit depolarizing channel is \[\mathcal D_q(\rho)=(1-q)\rho+\frac q3(X\rho X+Y\rho Y+Z\rho Z).\] The parameter \(q\) is the total probability of a nonidentity Pauli error. Capacity uses the operational definition below and is measured in qubits per independent channel use. The quantitative benchmark accepts a function with absolute error at most \(1/100\) throughout the whole domain.
definitions:
For the standard basis \(|0\rangle,|1\rangle\) of \(\mathbb C^2\), define \(X|0\rangle=|1\rangle\), \(X|1\rangle=|0\rangle\), \(Z|0\rangle=|0\rangle\), \(Z|1\rangle=-|1\rangle\), and \(Y=iXZ\), where \(i^2=-1\). Each of the three nonidentity errors has probability \(q/3\), and identity has probability \(1-q\). The formula therefore defines a channel for every real \(q\in[0,1]\). On general matrices it extends complex-linearly. In the coding definition, take \(A=B=\mathbb C^2\) and \(\Phi=\mathcal D_q\). The parameter is fixed across a code block and across the sequence of block lengths; a different parameter may have a different code sequence.

A density matrix on \(\mathbb C^d\) is a Hermitian matrix \(\rho=\rho^\dagger\) satisfying \(v^\dagger\rho v\ge0\) for every vector \(v\) and \(\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1\). Dagger denotes conjugate transpose and trace is the sum of diagonal entries. A quantum channel from \(\mathbb C^a\) to \(\mathbb C^b\) is a complex-linear map on matrices of the form \(\Psi(X)=\sum_j K_jXK_j^\dagger\), with finitely many \(b\)-by-\(a\) matrices obeying \(\sum_j K_j^\dagger K_j=I_a\). These are precisely the completely positive trace-preserving maps, abbreviated CPTP. Matrices in coding operations may have arbitrary complex entries. Memorylessness means that \(n\) uses of a fixed channel \(\Phi:A\to B\) act as the tensor power \(\Phi^{\otimes n}\), with independent noise and the same channel on every use.

For each integer \(n\ge1\), a code consists of a nonnegative integer \(k_n\), a CPTP encoder \(E_n\) from \(k_n\) qubits to \(A^{\otimes n}\), and a CPTP decoder \(D_n\) from \(B^{\otimes n}\) to \(k_n\) qubits. A qubit is a copy of \(\mathbb C^2\), so the message space has dimension \(2^{k_n}\). Let \[|\Omega_k\rangle=2^{-k/2}\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^k}|x\rangle_R\otimes|x\rangle_M\] be a maximally entangled unit vector between an untouched reference register \(R\) and a message register \(M\), each of dimension \(2^k\). For \(k=0\), both spaces are one-dimensional and the sum has one term. The entanglement fidelity of a code is \[F_n=\langle\Omega_{k_n}|\bigl[\operatorname{id}_R\otimes(D_n\circ\Phi^{\otimes n}\circ E_n)\bigr](|\Omega_{k_n}\rangle\langle\Omega_{k_n}|)|\Omega_{k_n}\rangle.\] The identity map leaves the reference unchanged, and \(\circ\) denotes composition, with the rightmost operation applied first. This tests preservation of quantum information and its correlations, rather than only classical basis labels.

A real rate \(r\ge0\) is achievable if there is a sequence of these codes, one for every \(n\ge1\), such that \(F_n\to1\) and \(\liminf_{n\to\infty}k_n/n\ge r\). Define \(Q(\Phi)\) as the supremum of achievable rates, in qubits per channel use. Rate zero is always achievable. The encoder and decoder may jointly process their entire blocks, use local ancillary systems and discard local systems. There is no bound on their computation or circuit sizes and no uniformity requirement on the sequence of codes. They depend on the channel but not on the unknown input message state. No preshared entanglement, additional classical communication, feedback or auxiliary quantum channel is supplied. The reference in the fidelity test is a mathematical test system, not a communication resource. The whole coding map is trace preserving: postselecting a successful event for free is not allowed. This is asymptotic, vanishing-error, unassisted quantum transmission capacity.
answer_criterion: Give an unambiguous real-valued function \(g:[0,1]\to\mathbb R\), together with a complete Lean-checked proof that \[|g(q)-Q(q)|\le\frac1{100}\qquad\text{for every real }q\in[0,1].\] The proof must establish both the lower and upper sides of this absolute error bound in qubits per channel use. Exact equality with \(Q\) also qualifies. A finite table, uncertified numerical plot, or restatement of the defining optimization or supremum does not determine the requested curve. There is no prescribed formula grammar, finite representation for the argument \(q\), or polynomial evaluation-time requirement. The inherited numerical acceptance is weaker than the source's exact-capacity question; a solution at this tolerance need not settle the exact positive-capacity threshold.
why: The unresolved communication limit of a canonical quantum-noise model. It tests whether quantum coding theory can turn regularized existence formulas into sharp quantitative limits despite degeneracy and multi-copy advantages.

importance.reason: A benchmark capacity problem connecting quantum error correction, information-theoretic converses and the operational effect of entangled encodings.

status_note: Uncertain for the inherited absolute 0.01 benchmark; the underlying exact-capacity question remains open in the checked primary literature. On 16 September 2026 the coding theorem, low-noise introduction, geometric bounds, May and August 2026 threshold results, and strong-converse statements were checked, together with current revision metadata and bounded later-work searches. No full curve meeting the benchmark was identified, but openness at that fixed tolerance was not independently established. The August certificate is a positivity lower bound, not an exact threshold or curve; its verification artifact was not run. No cited proof was independently verified or formalized in Lean.

context_blocks.text: Depolarizing noise treats the three Pauli errors symmetrically. Despite this short channel description, its quantum transmission limit allows arbitrary collective encodings over arbitrarily long blocks. The entanglement-fidelity criterion keeps the distinction between transmitting an unknown quantum state and sending only classical data.

Parameter conventions matter: the probabilities \((1-3p,p,p,p)\) correspond to \(p=q/3\). The expression \((1-\lambda)\rho+\lambda I/2\) has \(\lambda=4q/3\), with the usual convex-mixture interpretation only for \(q\le3/4\). Thus \(q=3/4\) is the completely depolarizing channel; \(q=1\) still specifies a valid channel, but is a different map. All thresholds here use total Pauli error \(q\).

The quantum coding theorem identifies the operational capacity with \(\sup_{n\ge1} n^{-1}\max_\rho I_c(\rho,\Phi^{\otimes n})\). Here \(\rho\) ranges over all input density matrices on \(A^{\otimes n}\). If \(|\psi\rangle\) is a purification of \(\rho\), meaning a unit vector on a reference and the input with input marginal \(\rho\), and \(\omega=(\operatorname{id}\otimes\Phi^{\otimes n})(|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|)\), then \(I_c=S(\omega_{B^{\otimes n}})-S(\omega)\). The marginal is obtained by tracing out the reference. For eigenvalues \(\lambda_j\) of a density matrix, \(S=-\sum_j\lambda_j\log_2\lambda_j\), with \(0\log_2 0=0\). The result is independent of the chosen purification. This exact regularized expression includes every block length; it is not an evaluation of the capacity curve or a finite stopping rule.

A known lower bound is \(\max\{0,1-h_2(q)-q\log_2 3\}\), where \(h_2(q)=-q\log_2q-(1-q)\log_2(1-q)\), with the endpoint convention \(0\log_2 0=0\). Its positive part vanishes near \(q=0.1893\). Multicopy results surpass this bound, so the one-use expression is not the capacity curve throughout the noise range.

Agarwal and coauthors report positive coherent information for a 45-copy symmetric rank-two input up to a numerically evaluated per-Pauli value \(p=0.064657\), corresponding to \(q=0.193971\). This is a lower bound from particular inputs, not optimality over all block lengths.

Krohn-Grimberghe supplies an exact-arithmetic certificate for a 45-copy state with positive coherent information at \(q=48717/250000=0.194868\). The paper also gives positivity below this point and distinguishes its certified witness from stronger numerical states in the earlier authors' repository. This review checked the statement, conventions and limitations; it did not rerun the supplied verification artifact.

The endpoints and a whole zero-capacity range are known: \(Q(0)=1\) and \(Q(q)=0\) for every \(q\ge1/4\). In that range the channel is antidegradable, meaning that a channel applied to the environment output can simulate the receiver's output. The certificate paper explicitly does not determine the true positivity threshold. Knowing that threshold alone would still not determine the positive-rate curve.
Leditzky, Leung and Smith determine low-noise capacities to leading orders. This controls an asymptotic regime near the noiseless channel and does not evaluate the whole parameter interval.

Zhu and coauthors give improved upper bounds for depolarizing channels. Their §3.4 retains a gap between achievable rates and upper bounds; a numerical comparison of bounds does not by itself certify the benchmark error throughout the domain.

The August 2026 strong-converse paper establishes fidelity decay above capacity for degradable and antidegradable channels and additional upper bounds. It explicitly distinguishes those bounds from an exact capacity value. A strong converse therefore does not supply the missing depolarizing curve.

The source literature retains the exact-capacity question. The absolute 0.01 acceptance rule was already adopted by the atlas before this review. Openness of the exact question does not alone imply that approximation to this tolerance is open; the status records that distinction.

sentences: A depolarizing channel models a qubit subjected to randomly chosen Pauli errors.
Its quantum capacity measures how much unknown quantum information can be transmitted reliably per channel use when many uses are encoded together.
The goal is the capacity curve throughout the noise range under the unassisted coding convention fixed in the card.
Coding across several uses can behave differently from optimizing a single use, which complicates attempts to match achievable rates with impossibility bounds.
The Lean benchmark accepts a certified determination with absolute error at most 0.01 throughout the stated numerical domain.
